newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peres and Arafat to discuss foundering peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Peres and Arafat to discuss foundering peace deal.

text.p: Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres will meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Sunday to discuss the peace deal that they nurtured and is now foundering.

Palestinian officials said Peres, ousted as prime minister by Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu in May elections, would hold talks with Arafat in the Israeli-blockaded West Bank town of Nablus at around 1100 GMT.
Netanyahu's spokesman said the prime minister had agreed to the talks between the two men, who last met on August 22.

U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross, mediating in talks between Israel and the Palestinians on implementing a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron, met Arafat in Nablus on Saturday.
"Obviously there are differences and we're trying to find the best way to overcome them," Ross told reporters afterwards.

Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters there was "not one inch of progress" in the Israeli-Palestinian talks and he urged Washington to push Israel to keep a deal reached by its previous government under Peres.
"We hope the U.S. administration and President Clinton will stop dealing with Israel as a state above the law," Erekat said.
The Hebron redeployment should have been carried out in March but was delayed by Peres after Islamic militant suicide bombings killed 59 people in Israel in February and March.

It was frozen by Netanyahu. He says changes are needed to the deal to ensure the security of 400 Jewish settlers living in Hebron, which has a population of 100,000 Arabs. The Palestinians refuse to amend the Hebron accord.
Several hundred Jewish settlers, demanding that Netanyahu must stand firm, on Saturday briefly blocked a road dividing Palestinian areas of Hebron from the Kiryat Arba Jewish settlement.
A leader of the outlawed anti-Arab Kach movement, Baruch Merzel who lives in Hebron, earlier warned of an explosion of violence if Israel redeployed its forces in the town.

Israel, which tightened an entry ban against Palestinians after clashes last month, had said that 35,000 workers would be allowed into Israel on Sunday. But Palestinian officials said Israel had so far given them only 4,400 permits to issue.
The Israeli media reported that 33 Israeli reserve soldiers had written an open letter to Netanyahu warning him against involving the Jewish state in a war.

"The fighting spirit and the readiness to sacrifice are conditioned on the knowledge that the government is doing all it can in order to prevent war," said an excerpt of the letter broadcast on Israel's Channel Two television.
"In light of recent developments, we have been cut off from that fighting spirit, without which we do not see how we can take part in the next war."
